question: Which definition best describes a functional interface in Java 17?
options: An interface that declares no methods
An interface annotated with @FunctionalInterface, whatever it declares
An interface that has exactly one abstract method
An interface that declares exactly one method of any kind
explanation: A functional interface is defined by its shape: exactly one abstract method (not counting default, static, private, or public Object-method redeclarations). The annotation is only a compile-time check and is not what makes an interface functional.

question: What is the effect of placing @FunctionalInterface on an interface?
options: The compiler verifies that the interface has exactly one abstract method and reports an error otherwise
The interface becomes usable as a lambda target; without it, lambdas cannot be assigned to it
All methods of the interface automatically become default methods
The JVM generates an implementing class at compile time
explanation: The annotation is a safety net that makes the compiler enforce the single-abstract-method rule. An unannotated interface with one abstract method is still a valid lambda target. The trap is believing the annotation is required.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: Compile-time error because Shape has two abstract methods but is annotated as functional
It compiles, but a runtime error occurs when Shape is loaded
It compiles with only a warning and prints x

question: Which of the following cannot be the target type of a lambda expression?
options: An abstract class that declares exactly one abstract method
A custom interface with one abstract method and one static method
explanation: Lambda targets must be functional interfaces. An abstract class is never a valid target, even with a single abstract method; use an anonymous class instead.

question: Which statement best summarizes how default and static methods affect whether an interface is functional?
options: They count toward the single-method limit just like abstract methods
They do not count; only abstract methods are counted
Default methods are allowed but static methods make the interface non-functional
A functional interface cannot declare either of them
explanation: Only abstract methods (excluding public Object-method redeclarations) are counted. An interface can have any number of default, static, and private methods and still be functional.

question: Why does this code fail to compile?

question: Which statement best describes the function type of a functional interface's abstract method?
options: Its parameter types, return type, and throws clause describe the shape a compatible lambda must fit
Its method name must appear inside the lambda body
Its return type must always be void
It must be declared static so a lambda can call it
explanation: A lambda is checked against the abstract method's parameter types, return type, and allowed checked exceptions. The method name is irrelevant to the lambda.

explanation: A lambda body may throw only the checked exceptions its functional method declares. Runnable.run declares none, so the unhandled InterruptedException from Thread.sleep is a compile-time error.

question: A lambda must call a method that throws java.io.IOException and return a String. Which interface can be the lambda's target without catching the exception inside the lambda?
options: interface Source { String get() throws RuntimeException; }
interface Source { String get() throws java.io.IOException; }
interface Source { default String get() throws java.io.IOException { return ""; } }
explanation: The abstract method must declare a throws clause that permits IOException. A RuntimeException clause does not permit IOException, and a default method is not abstract, so that interface would not be functional.

question: Comparator declares both compare(T, T) and equals(Object) as abstract methods, yet it is a functional interface. Why?
options: equals matches a public method of Object, so it is not counted as an abstract method
equals is implemented as a default method in Comparator
equals is declared static in Comparator
Comparator is functional only because it is annotated
explanation: Redeclarations of public Object methods are excluded from the abstract-method count because every implementing class already inherits an implementation from Object.

question: An unannotated interface Handler has one abstract method and is used by many lambdas. A developer adds a second abstract method and recompiles the project. What happens to the existing lambdas?
options: They keep compiling; the new method returns a default value
They keep compiling but throw AbstractMethodError when called
They fail to compile because Handler is no longer a functional interface
They compile only if converted to method references

options: A lambda can replace an anonymous class of any interface
A lambda can replace an anonymous subclass of an abstract class with one abstract method

options: A lambda is a new primitive function type independent of interfaces

question: Which local variables can a lambda expression capture from its enclosing method?

question: Which statement best explains why Java requires captured local variables to be effectively final?
